authorHeadline: SSE @Oracle | ex Amazon | ex Microsoft | Best Selling Udemy Instructor | IIT KGP || Heartfulness Meditation Trainer
content: Right now, AI is throwing so much at developers that I am almost certain most of us have had some version of this thought:"Do I actually know enough anymore?"The models keep changing. The tools keep changing. Someone on Twitter is running 15 agents at once. Someone else is building things in a weekend that used to take a team weeks.You are working harder and faster, but somehow still feel behind.I have felt that too.I felt it when I was an intern at Amazon. I felt it again after joining full-time. And even after spending years around very strong engineers, that feeling still shows up sometimes.The difference now is that I understand it better.Software engineering is too large for anyone to know everything. You can spend years with one language and still find parts of it you have never touched. Add databases, distributed systems, cloud, security, AI agents, and the gap between what you know and what exists becomes enormous.Then the internet makes it worse.We see someone's best project, promotion, offer, benchmark, or perfectly working demo.We don't see the three days they were stuck on one bug.We don't see the design they got completely wrong.We don't see the senior engineer opening documentation for something they have used for years.So your brain compares your behind-the-scenes struggle with everyone else's highlight reel.That comparison will destroy your confidence if you let it.For me, imposter syndrome has slowly become less about "I am not good enough" and more about "I have reached something I don't understand yet."You don't need to know everything before you belong in the room.You need enough humility to say "I don't know," enough curiosity to learn it, and enough confidence to keep working while you figure it out.AI has made the field faster.It has not made any of us all-knowing. We are all still learning.… moreA lot of confidence comes from surviving enough “I have no idea what I’m doing” moments. You eventually notice that the feeling does not predict the outcome. You have felt lost before and still figured it out.… more

content: I spent the last 2 months in San Francisco, and I was there when some of these layoffs were announced. Yes, the AI boom is real but a lot of it is hype and marketing gimmicks as well.The AI gains are real, no doubt but so is the burnout that no seems to be talking about. I know this because I met engineers at Google and Microsoft, spent time around Cursor, visited GitHub HQ, and spoke to a lot of founders, managers, and engineers.Everyone is excited about what AI can do.But behind that excitement, a lot of people are exhausted.And I think there are 3 things happening at the same time.1. Companies are spending insane amounts of money on AICompute, GPUs, data centers, model access, infra, talent.That money has to come from somewhere.So teams are getting flattened, roles are getting merged, and companies are trying to see how much more output they can get from fewer people.That is part of why layoffs and restructuring keep showing up.2. The people who remain are carrying moreA team that had 10 people becomes 6.But the deliverables are now 3-4x more. So now those 6 people are expected to move faster, ship more, review more code, and maintain the same quality.I heard versions of this again and again.People are tired.Not lazy. Not resistant to AI.Genuinely tired.3. Then we tell those same people to "upskill"This is the part that bothers me.An engineer finishes a long day, handles production issues, reviews agent-generated code, attends meetings, and then the internet says:"Learn agents.""Learn evals.""Learn MCP.""Learn the new model.""Upskill or get left behind."When exactly?Evals are becoming basic knowledge for anyone building serious AI products, and I still meet good engineers who barely have time to learn them properly because their current workload is already eating the whole day.That is the weird place tech is in right now.Teams are shrinking.Expectations are rising.The tools are improving faster than people have time to learn them.And everyone feels guilty for not keeping up.SF feels incredibly optimistic about AI right now.But underneath that optimism, there are a lot of very capable people running on fumes.I think both things can be true at once.AI can make us far more productive.And the way companies are chasing that productivity can make the people doing the work absolutely exhausted.… more“Upskill after work” sounds very reasonable until you describe the actual day. Eight hours of coding, meetings, debugging, reviewing AI output, production issues, maybe commute and family. Then at 10 PM somebody on Twitter tells you that you are falling behind because you have not learned the agent framework released on Tuesday. Of course people are tired.… more

content: “We’ll pay you.” Student: “That sounds suspicious.”It is funny until you remember why someone would even think that way.For years, a strange category of "internships" became normal in India where students were asked to pay registration fees, training fees, security deposits, or some other made-up charge just to work for someone.And students still paid.Because they were scared.Scared that without an internship certificate their resume would look empty.Scared that everyone else was getting experience while they were falling behind.Scared that saying no would cost them their first real opportunity.Some of them then worked long hours, did actual company work, got treated poorly, and still had to pay for it.That has completely damaged the meaning of "paid internship."Now when someone says "this is a paid internship," some students genuinely wonder: "Paid by whom?"That is such a broken trust signal.Thankfully, students are more aware now, and these scams get called out much faster than they used to.But rebuilding trust takes longer than destroying it.So yes, the screenshot is hilarious.But for someone who has already been exploited once, the confusion makes complete sense.We somehow managed to reach a point where "we will pay you" sounds like the suspicious part.That should tell us how badly the system was abused.… more“Certificate milega” did a lot of damage. Students were so scared of having nothing on the resume that even a meaningless PDF started feeling worth paying for. That is how the whole thing became normal. … more

authorHeadline: Co Founder & CEO at Joy
content: In 1997, I wanted to learn about artificial intelligence. I did not own a computer.I was a first-year electrical engineering student at NIT Rourkela when a library book made me curious about how computers could learn.So I went to Prof. Ganapati Panda, who was researching AI, and asked if I could work with him.I knew very little and was not in his department. He said no, but I kept returning every few weeks.After six or seven months, he gave me a problem involving partial differentiation and neural networks. If I could solve it, he would let me work with him.When campus emptied for the break, I stayed to work on it.PhD students, including Dr. Debi Prasad Das, let me use their labs and patiently helped me work through things I did not understand.About a month later, I brought Prof. Panda a solution.That led to three years of research on neural networks for active noise cancellation. Some of that work involved trying to cancel the noise from a moped.Looking back, having a specific problem made an enormous difference."Learn artificial intelligence" was an ambition I barely knew how to act on. A problem gave me somewhere to begin.When I got stuck, I had something specific to look up or ask about. The mathematics made more sense because I was trying to use it.And I had people around me who were willing to spend time helping a beginner.I was curious, and I hoped this might help me build a better life for my family. I had no idea where any of it would lead.What I appreciate more now is how much time those people gave me when I had very little to offer in return. They had their own research to do, but they still made room for mine.I hope I remember that the next time someone asks me for a chance. Giving them a problem they can work on, then being available when they get stuck, may be more useful than giving them advice.… more

content: Redis add করতে বসলাম। Architecture ও বড় হচ্ছে। তারপর একটা প্রশ্ন করলাম নিজেকে — আসলে কী slow, সেটা কি measure করেছি?"Caching add করলে fast হয়" — এটাই ছিল আমার সবচেয়ে বড় blind spot। প্রতিটা performance article এ caching থাকে, তাই মনে হয় add করতেই হবে। কিন্তু কখন করতে হবে, কেন করতে হবে — সেটা কেউ বলে না।Cache add করা সহজ। গুরুত্বপূর্ণ হলো এটা জানা কখন cached value আর valid না। Computer science এ বিখ্যাত একটা কথা আছে: দুটো জিনিস সত্যিই hard — cache invalidation আর naming things। Joke মনে হয়, কিন্তু production এ গিয়ে বুঝা যায় এটা joke না।আগে এই দুটো প্রশ্ন — Operation টা কি expensive? মানে 200ms+ লাগছে, external API call হচ্ছে, heavy computation হচ্ছে? আর result টা কি stable? মানে store করার পর return করার আগেই বদলে যাবে না? দুটোর উত্তর হ্যাঁ না হলে cache করার কোনো কারণ নেই।তিনটা জায়গায় cache হতে পারে। Client এ — browser নিজেই response store করে, পরের request এ network এই যায় না। সবচেয়ে efficient, কিন্তু শুধু static data র জন্য। Application memory তে — code এর ভেতরেই dictionary তে store করো, external কিছু লাগে না। Problem হলো multiple instance থাকলে প্রতিটার আলাদা cache, আর restart এ সব গায়েব। Redis বা external cache এ — সব instance share করে, restart এ থাকে। কিন্তু এটা আলাদা infrastructure, আলাদা cost, আলাদা complexity।Cache Invalidation কেন hard — Store করা easy। দুটো approach আছে। Time-based — নির্দিষ্ট সময় পর expire হয়। Simple, কিন্তু trade-off আছে: short expiry মানে বেশি cache miss, long expiry মানে stale data। Event-based — data change হলে explicitly cache delete করো। Consistent, কিন্তু data যেখানে যেখানে change হতে পারে সব জায়গায় invalidation logic লিখতে হবে। একটা miss মানে stale data, debug করা nightmare।আমি actually cache add করিনি। API তে সবচেয়ে expensive operation ছিল OCR আর AI API call — প্রতিটা different image, cache করার কোনো উপায় নেই। বাকি queries ছিল 20-30ms এর। Redis add করলে operational cost, invalidation logic, consistency risk — সব আসতো। কিন্তু কোনো real problem solve হতো না।এটাই decision framework। Theoretical performance gain এর জন্য না, real measured problem এর জন্য cache করো।কখন করবো তাহলে? যখন database measurably slow হবে real load এ — benchmark এ না। যখন external API বারবার same data return করবে। যখন monitoring দেখাবে specific endpoint এ users latency feel করছে। সব ক্ষেত্রেই আগে measure, তারপর decision।Inefficient query এর উপর cache বসালে problem solve হয় না — লুকিয়ে যায়। Cache remove হলে original problem আবার বের হয়, এখন cache layer ও maintain করতে হচ্ছে।"Caching add করলে fast হয়" বলা আর বোঝা যে cache একটা complexity যেটাকে justify করতে হয় — সম্পূর্ণ আলাদা জিনিস।তোমার app এ কি কোনো cache আছে যেটা আসলে দরকার ছিল না? content: In the last 6 months, I have spent 100s of hours working with coding agents, with some weeks stretching to 10+ hour workdays. And one thing still annoys me more than almost anything: I ask for a 3-line fix.The agent gives me a slop 500 line output or a refactor I never asked for. After enough of this, I have 6 defaults now.[1] Say "minimal change" explicitlyMy prompt starts with something like: "Work only this function. No new files. No refactor. Stop when the failing case passes."Agents do much better when the boundary is part of the task.[2] Define done before it starts"Test X passes, then stop."Without a stop condition, long-horizon agents keep finding work to do. [3] Keep AGENTS.md tinyI used to think more context meant better output. It often means more wandering.Keep only project-specific rules, invariants, and things the model repeatedly gets wrong. [4] Match the model to the jobA 3-line hotfix does not need your frontier-level model, five subagents, and maximum reasoning.Save the heavy machinery for migrations, large refactors, and long tasks.[5] Reduce the blast radiusNew branch. One task. File allowlist. Commit before the run.If it decides your bugfix needs a new architecture, deleting the branch should take 2 seconds.[6] Review the diff, not the confidenceAgents can write tests that happily approve their own bad assumptions.I care about:→ Did it work on only what I asked?→ Did it change behaviour anywhere else?→ Can I explain every added line?→ Is this genuinely the smallest fix?Also, you should explore these repos for more help: 1. content: Job security in 2026 doesn't exist, just look at the state of the job market. But that does not mean everyone should take the highest-paying offer and figure out the consequences later.A 25-year-old who is single, has low expenses, and can move back home if something goes wrong is playing a very different game from a 35-year-old supporting parents, a spouse, two kids, school fees, and a home loan.The same $100K remote offer can be a brilliant decision for one person and an unnecessary risk for another.That is why I would never judge unambitious for choosing stability.Yes, startups can give you insane upside. You learn faster, own more, work closer to the business, and right now people with strong AI skills are getting opportunities that may look completely different five years from now.But risk only makes sense when you can survive the downside.If your entire household depends on your salary, you naturally care about runway, health insurance, predictable income, and what happens if the startup loses funding six months later.That is responsibility, I wouldn't call that fear.And if someone is good enough to land a $100K remote role once, chances are they can find another high-quality opportunity that better matches the risk they are comfortable taking.I think the mistake is turning career decisions into some universal rule:"Always join startups.""Never leave big tech.""Take the money.""Choose stability."None of these work for everyone.Look at your responsibilities. Look at your savings. Look at how replaceable your current income is. Look at the upside you are giving up and the downside you would actually have to live through.Then decide.Careers are personal because consequences of the decisions are personal too. content: The struggles of Scrum Master with bigger team:Being a Scrum Master for a team of 5 is a completely different game than managing a team of 12+.When a Scrum team scales past the sweet spot (5–9 people), standard ceremonies start to break down if you don't actively adapt.Here are the biggest struggles Scrum Masters face with oversized teams—and how to navigate them:1. The Daily Standup turns into a marathon 🏃‍♂️With 12+ people, 15 minutes quickly turns into 30. It stops being a quick tactical sync on the Sprint Goal and transforms into a tedious status report.👉 Shift: Encourage sub-team syncs or run asynchronous check-ins for routine updates, reserving live standup time strictly for blockers and goal alignment.2. Backlog Refinement becomes chaotic 📋Getting 14 people to focus on a single user story breakdown leads to disengagement, side conversations, and mental fatigue.👉 Shift: Break the team into dynamic working groups during refinement. Let 3-4 engineers focus on breaking down specific epics, then share back with the wider team.3. Psychological safety quietly disappears 🛡️In large groups, introverted team members get swallowed up while vocal voices dominate the room. Retrospectives lose their raw honesty.👉 Shift: Use silent brainstorming tools (like Miro or LocalRetro) and asynchronous voting before opening the floor for discussion.4. Mini-waterfalls start forming inside the Sprint 🌊Large teams struggle with cross-functionality, leading to internal hand-off delays between developers and QA before the Sprint ends.👉 Shift: Align team members around micro-outcomes or small feature pods rather than individual discipline silos.💡 The Key TakeawayScrum wasn't designed for crowd control. content: 30 agent security patterns every security engineer should know:IDENTITY & ACCESS1. Agent identities ↳ Give every agent a verifiable identity.2. Least privilege ↳ Grant only the access its task needs.3. Short-lived tokens ↳ Expire access quickly.4. Scoped delegation ↳ Keep delegated access within the caller’s permissions.5. Step-up authentication ↳ Reverify identity before sensitive actions.TOOLS & EXECUTION6. Tool allowlists ↳ Expose only approved tools.7. Argument validation ↳ Validate parameters, paths, and destinations in code.8. Action authorization ↳ Check permissions at the service executing each action.9. Human approval gates ↳ Show what will happen before asking for approval.10. Output sanitization ↳ Handle tool and model outputs safely before reuse.CONTEXT & RETRIEVAL11. Instruction isolation ↳ Separate trusted instructions from untrusted data.12. Untrusted content labels ↳ Mark external content without treating labels as protection.13. Permission-aware retrieval ↳ Retrieve only data the requesting user can access.14. Source provenance ↳ Track where retrieved information came from.15. Memory write gates ↳ Control what gets stored and who can change it.ISOLATION & BOUNDARIES16. Sandboxed execution ↳ Run agent code inside a restricted environment.17. Filesystem scoping ↳ Limit access to the files each task needs.18. Egress allowlists ↳ Restrict outbound network destinations.19. Tenant isolation ↳ Separate customer data, memory, and execution.20. Secret brokering ↳ Inject credentials outside the model’s context.PROTOCOL & SUPPLY CHAIN21. MCP server verification ↳ Verify server identity before connecting.22. Token audience checks ↳ Reject tokens intended for another service.23. Dependency pinning ↳ Lock reviewed versions and update deliberately.24. Tool-change review ↳ Review changes to tool behavior and permissions.25. Session binding ↳ Bind sessions to authenticated identities.DETECTION & RECOVERY26. Audit trails ↳ Record actions, approvals, and permission changes.27. Adversarial evals ↳ Test hostile inputs and unauthorized action attempts.28. Resource budgets ↳ Cap runtime, tool calls, tokens, and spending.29. Kill switches ↳ Stop runs and revoke access quickly.30. Checkpoint rollback ↳ Restore trusted state. External actions may need separate recovery.Start with the tools your agent can call.What can each tool read, change, or send? Who authorizes that action? How would you stop it?Enforce those answers in code. content: How Should You Present Yourself in a PhD Application in the USA? 🇺🇸A PhD application is more than a GPA, test score, or list of achievements. Your application should help the admissions committee see you as a potential researcher.There are two important stages:1 - Your written applicationSOP: Don’t write an autobiography. Explain your research interests, previous experience, future goals, and why you are interested in that program and faculty.CV: Clearly present your research experience, publications, projects, technical skills, presentations, awards, and other academic achievements. Recommendation Letters: Choose professors who know your work well and can genuinely speak about your research ability, independence, and academic potential.2 - Your interviewIf you are invited for an interview, the committee already knows your academic background from your application. Now they want to understand how you think, communicate, discuss research, handle questions, and work with others.If you present your previous research, be prepared to explain:🔹 What problem did you address?🔹 Why was it important?🔹 What methods did you use?🔹 What did you find?🔹 What did you learn?🔹 What could be done next?If you don't know an answer, don't panic. Be honest and explain how you would approach the question.And remember faculty fit. Don't simply say that a university is highly ranked. Explain why the professor's research and the program are relevant to your goals.A strong PhD application should clearly answer:- What have you done?- What do you want to research?- Why are you a good fit?Your goal is not to appear perfect. I've learned this the stupid and hard way.At one point I had 14 agents running across 3 dev servers.And it was beautiful.But in practice, I was constantly thinking:→ Which one finished?→ Which one is blocked?→ Which one is waiting for me?→ Which agent is debugging this?→ What was I supposed to review next?I literally started naming them because I could no longer remember who was doing what.The agents were working in parallel.However, my brain was carrying all of their state.That was the problem.So the biggest improvement I made was changing the environment around the models.Now I mostly talk to one central agent, my Wingman. It breaks work into small chunks, coordinates the other agents and brings things back to me when a decision is actually needed.And I have become much more deliberate about three things:→ Give every agent a very clear boundary.→ Make handoffs tell me what changed, what was checked and what is still uncertain.→ Separate “still working” from “needs me right now.”That last is very important. If every agent feels like something I should check every five minutes, then I have just created 14 new notifications for myself.I still catch myself doing this. My wife has literally asked why I keep walking back into the study.and my reply, “I’m checking my agents.” (Yep, does me no favours, haha)So I have not completely solved it.But I have learned one thing: The goal of an agent setup is not to keep more work running.It is to let more work run without keeping all of it running inside your head.So, if you're running agents, spend time on your environment and your workflow, you might not even need stronger models, these small fixes can give you a huge boost. … moreBatch review makes sense because review itself needs concentration. If I review one agent change, then answer another agent, then return to the first diff, I have lost the mental model I was building. Three clean reviews in one block can be easier than three “quick” reviews spread across the afternoon.… more

authorHeadline: Co-founder @ hellointerview.com
content: We use Temporal extensively at Hello Interview and really like it. I think it's incredibly useful to know for both system design interviews and day-to-day backend work.We use it for all our critical workflows that need to complete reliably, from payment flows to long-running AI evaluation pipelines.Without Temporal, these workflows often turn into some combination of queues, retry logic, scheduled jobs, state tables, and code that figures out where to resume after something fails.Temporal lets you model that whole process as a workflow in code. It persists the workflow's progress as it runs, so if a worker dies halfway through, another can reconstruct where it was and keep going.That’s why it’s such a useful primitive in system design interviews too. Instead of hand-waving over retries, state machines, cron jobs, and recovery logic, you can talk concretely about how a long-running workflow survives failure.And in production, the same abstraction can replace a surprising amount of custom orchestration code.We just published a new deep dive covering how Temporal works, including Workflows, Activities, replay, determinism, retries, timers, Signals, and the architecture underneath it.Give it a read!https://lnkd.in/gVFWdsT4… moreI totally get the context Evan, but temporal is too niche and the interviewer might not know what temporal is?temporal vs airflow vs dagster. content: Vibe coding can get software moving fast. The real engineering challenge starts when that software has to survive scale, changing requirements, multiple teams, production incidents, security reviews, and years of continuous development.That is where shortcuts become expensive. A feature that works today can still leave behind tightly coupled logic, unclear boundaries, fragile integrations, inconsistent patterns, and technical decisions that make every next release harder than the last.The problem is not using AI to write code faster. We use it too.The problem is treating code generation as a substitute for software engineering.Production-grade software still needs deliberate architecture, clear domain boundaries, strong engineering standards, automated testing, observability, security, and engineers who understand the consequences of the decisions being made underneath the interface.That is the difference between software that simply works now and software your team can confidently extend, operate, and scale later.At Craftsmen, we combine AI-native development with the engineering discipline required to build and evolve serious software products.So if you need to move fast without sacrificing the engineering discipline your software will depend on later, we’re ready to help with our AI-native engineering team.… moreVibe coding is basically a form of prototyping. But prototyping and building a complex system are two very different things.Nevertheless, if you first develop a solid architecture and use it as a skeleton on which to put the vibe-coded meat—backed by regression testing and tight control over individual components—you can build a better system, more quickly and easily, than through traditional manual programming alone.Manual programming as the primary way of building software is becoming a thing of the past. authorHeadline: Co Founder & CEO at Joy
content: When I left Microsoft to start Joy, I told myself that if it failed, I could work at a Walmart cash register and still be okay.I had spent more than a decade at Microsoft, including on Azure's founding team. The work mattered to me, and the salary once felt unimaginable. Microsoft even offered me stock to stay.There were plenty of good reasons to stay.But Dorian, Kaiwalya, and I wanted to build Joy. I kept thinking about how I would feel years later if we never tried.Jeff Bezos calls this the "regret minimization framework." In a 2010 Princeton address, he said he could accept trying and failing, but never trying might haunt him.It was a useful question after working so hard for the life I was considering leaving.I waited until I had my green card. I needed the right to stay and work in the country if Joy failed. Beyond that, leaving felt like putting almost all my chips back on the table.The Walmart thought did not mean starting over would be easy. It helped me make peace with the possibility.We went without salaries for four years because wedding technology was hard to fund and the money had to last. People called us nuts. I understood why.I also put off telling my parents. They had sacrificed to help me build this life. When I finally told them, they understood. They trusted us with a decision whose outcome none of us could know.Today, Joy is used in more than 150 countries. More than 250 million people have used it, and over 2 million events have been planned on it.We could not have imagined that reach when we started. I still do not think we're where we want to be.I would not make this choice for anyone else. We all have responsibilities to take seriously.But if something has stayed on your mind for years, the possibility of never trying deserves a place in the decision too.There were still very good reasons to stay on the day I left.There was also enough reason to try.Maybe it is time to give the thing you keep thinking about a real chance.… more

content: The internet has completely messed with our sense of time.I landed my first software engineering job in 2006.It took me until 2010 to get into Amazon.And I did not get into Google until 2022.None of those jumps happened overnight.But if I were 22 today and spent enough time online, I might genuinely feel like I was already behind.Because every day you see someone saying:→ Become Staff Engineer before 30→ Retire at 35→ Build a startup by 20→ Make ₹2 lakh/month by 25After a while, normal progress starts feeling slow.That is the problem.Urgency is useful when it gets you moving.Too much urgency makes every year feel like failure.You start rushing through skills that need depth.You switch directions before anything compounds.You compare your year 2 with someone else's year 12.And then you wonder why nothing feels enough.Hard things usually take time.Becoming genuinely good at engineering takes years.Building financial stability takes years.Getting healthy takes time.Learning how to lead people takes time.Even the people who look "naturally talented" usually have years of invisible work behind them. Yes, some people move unusually fast.That does not mean your life should be planned around being an outlier.One thing I understand much better after almost 20 years in tech is that career and life stack up in very boring ways.A few skills get stronger.Your judgment improves.You meet better people.You make fewer stupid mistakes.Then one day someone looks at where you are and calls it an overnight success.So have urgency about starting.But have patience about becoming.Don’t think you’re slow, just give difficult things enough time to actually work.… moreOne thing the internet completely destroyed is the ability to enjoy a milestone for more than 24 hoursyou get the job you wantedyou got the result you wantednext morning someone younger posts a bigger package and suddenly your own win feels smallerthat is such a stupid habit people have installed in their heads… more

content: Best Android Engineers would fail a LeetCodeAnd some of the best LeetCode performers I have interviewed couldn't architect a production Android app.That's a problem: LeetCode tests how well you can solve an abstract problem under time pressure.Production Android engineering requires a much broader set of skills:→ Understanding lifecycle, memory, threading, and performance→ Designing for unreliable networks and real devices→ Debugging issues that don't reproduce locally→ Handling race conditions and concurrency problems→ Making architectural decisions that survive changing requirements→ Managing technical debt without bringing development to a halt→ Understanding trade-offs instead of searching for a single "correct" answer→ Working with product, backend, QA, design, and other engineers👉 I have never needed to invert a binary tree in production, but I have spent hours tracking down a coroutine race condition that only happened under a very specific sequence of events.👉 I have never had a production incident because I couldn't solve a dynamic programming problem in 30 minutes, but I have had to make architectural decisions where there was no perfect answer, only trade-offs.So if you are hiring Android engineers, maybe there are better signals to evaluate alongside algorithms:"Tell me about the hardest production bug you have solved.""Design an architecture for a real product and explain your trade-offs.""Here is a PR. What would you change and why?""Tell me about an architectural decision you would make differently today.""How would you investigate a performance issue affecting a small percentage of users?"I'm not saying algorithms don't matter: They do.Problem-solving, data structures, and algorithms are valuable engineering skills, but a timed LeetCode Hard shouldn't be the primary filter for someone whose actual job is to build, debug, scale, and maintain production applications.Maybe the better question isn't:"Can this developer solve this problem in 30 minutes?"Maybe it's:"Can this developer solve the problems our users will actually have?"What are your thoughts?#Android #AndroidDevelopment #LeetCode #CodingInterviews #SoftwareEngineering #MobileDevelopment #TechInterviews #Kotlin #CMP #KMP… moreAs a business owner how would you filter out quality engineers from the noise. especially when the market so saturated. you gotta put harder filters to extract that one candidate who beats hundreds of others

content: In 2013, when I finished my B.tech, I never thought I would be sitting at a college induction again. 13 years later, I was proved very wrong. A few days ago, I was invited to the induction at Polaris School of Technology in Bangalore. This time I was on the other side, answering questions from students and parents.The vibes were immaculate, mind you, and the energy just hit different. For a moment, it took me back to my own experiences as a student and how incredibly the world has changed, from learning to teaching to the whole industry. And Polaris is no different; they’re also doing things so differently for their students. → More focus on building, instead of an outdated syllabus→ More exposure to people actually working in the industry→ More conversations around skills, careers, projects, and what companies expect outside the classroomThe gap between "having a CSE degree" and "being ready to be hired" has become much wider in the industry, and I’m glad we have colleges now with a builder mindset. The whole event had an incredible mix of talented people from all over the industry. I got to meet and hear from leaders like Govinda Sambamurthy from Salesforce, Venkatesan Vaidhyanathan from Slice,Ashlin Joseph from Myntra, Aayushi from Amazon, Mino Thomas from Adobe, Alekhya Chakrabarty from InfoEdge,Shivendra Yadav from HCLTech, and many more people across engineering, talent, startups, and education.But something else happened that I was not expecting. So many students and parents came up to me during the event and said they already knew me from LinkedIn or Twitter.Some had been reading my posts for months. Some remembered my journey from old posts. I was so pleasantly surprised. A little over a year ago, I was mostly just an engineer sharing things I had learned from my own career. Today, I’m an inspiration to some people, and that in itself is so huge for me. Martin, the guy who literally wrote Clean Code, says he no longer reviews every line his agents write.I have stopped writing code by hand. I barely use an IDE anymore.And somehow, we are doing more engineering than ever.The state of software engineering in 2026 is definitely unexpected to say the least. 1. The IDE is no longer the center of the job.My day is increasingly spent describing problems, splitting work across agents, giving them context, checking what comes back and deciding what actually gets shipped.2. Code review is changing completely.Uncle Bob trusts a wall of tests, metrics and constraints.I am more conservative. I still read important diffs because I have tried delegating that review and I am not comfortable with the results yet.But nobody can manually inspect every line when agents can generate thousands of them while you sleep.3. AI productivity also means more work.I have had 14 agents running across 3 dev servers. That does not mean I am relaxing while they work.The exhaustion moves from typing code to keeping track of everything that is moving. My fix has been to set up a central coordinator agent, I call my agent, wingman. 4. Understanding the system is getting harder.Writing code used to force you to understand it.Now an agent can jump over all of that and hand you working code.So I have deliberately put learning back into the process: trace requests, read important diffs, ask why, understand failures and keep rebuilding the mental model.5. Even the way we give agents context is changing.Dumping everything into one giant context window is already becoming a bad habit.Keep the permanent context small. Put repeatable workflows into skills. Load knowledge when the agent actually needs it.And through all of this, software engineering jobs have not disappeared.The market is still hiring. The work is still there.What changed is what the engineer spends the day doing.I think tests are going to become more important, but also easier to misuse.An agent can misunderstand the requirement, implement the wrong thing, then write a beautiful test suite proving its wrong interpretation works perfectly.So the real question becomes: who defined what “correct” means before the agent started coding?… more

People who spent all those painful hours are, ironically, some of the best vibe coders today, haha.And I think it's because of two things:→ After you have debugged enough bad code, "it works" stops being enough. content: time to report a success!that's right! 200 OKtime to report a failure!that's right! 200 OKIf you want to become S-tier at API design during System Design interviews, keep these 20 things in your head:1. Before designing endpoints, ask what the user is actually trying to do2. Use nouns for resources: /users, /orders, /payments3. Do not make every action a random POST request4. If the same request happens twice, ask what breaks5. Payments, bookings, orders: think idempotency immediately6. Never return 50,000 rows because "the DB can handle it"7. Use cursor pagination when data keeps changing8. Decide what happens when two people update the same thing together9. Authentication answers "who are you?" Authorization answers "are you allowed?"10. Put rate limits around anything people can abuse11. Every external call needs a timeout12. Every retry needs a limit, backoff, and some randomness13. If work takes minutes, return a job ID instead of keeping HTTP open14. Tell clients why something failed, not only 400 Bad Request15. Think about what can safely be cached and how stale it can become16. Do not expose your database design directly through the API17. For webhooks, assume delivery can happen twice or arrive late18. Add request IDs because debugging distributed systems without them is pain19. Avoid versioning everything on day one, but know how you will handle breaking changes20. For every important endpoint, ask: what happens at 100x traffic and what happens when one dependency dies?---Btw, If you're preparing for technical interviews, check out: https://layrs.me/library

content: You do not need to have served 100 million users to learn how systems behave at 100 million users. Yes, I know it almost doesn’t make sense. You see, you need to learn how to look at the system you already know and see what changes as the pressure increases.That is the skill being tested.So, if you’re wondering the same thing that I haven’t worked at Google or Atlassian scale, how am I supposed to answer questions like that? Start here: [1] Start with something you have actually builtTake one API from your current job.Maybe it does 100 requests per second today.Now see:→ What happens at 1,000?→ What happens at 10,000?→ Does the app server run out of CPU first?→ Does the DB connection pool fill up?→ Does one query become too slow as the table grows?→ Does a downstream API become the bottleneck?This exercise is very useful. You are learning where pressure moves through a system.Btw, if you want to go deeper on these fundamentals, I’ve put 90+ of them together into my System Design Fundamentals Guide for Senior to Principal-level interview prep.You can check it out here: puneetpatwari.in[2] Follow one request all the way throughTake a normal request and trace it:client → gateway → service → cache → database → queue → worker → dependencyA system does not suddenly fail because you got too much traffic. It’s usually because something bounded became saturated.[3] Learn the common moves, but always learn the costIf reads get slow:→ add indexes→ cache hot data→ use replicas→ precompute expensive resultsIf writes become hot:→ partition→ batch→ reduce coordinationIf slow work blocks the request:→ push it to a queueIf one customer dominates:→ isolate that tenantBut every solution creates another problem.Caching gives you invalidation.Replication gives you stale reads.Queues give you retries and duplicate delivery.Sharding gives you rebalancing and hot partitions.[4] Use numbers to decide where depth is neededYou need enough math to know when the simple design stops being believable.Estimate:→ peak QPS→ read/write ratio→ payload size→ daily storage growth→ expected latency→ concurrencyIf the system gets 50 writes per second, you probably do not need a complicated distributed write architecture.If it gets 500,000 writes per second, now partitioning, batching, replication, and backpressure deserve a serious discussion.That is really how I would prepare. Take the systems you already understand and keep asking:… moreI like thinking of capacity as budgets.Database has a connection budget.Downstream API has a QPS budget.Queue consumers have a processing budget.Once you think this way, the design question becomes: what happens when demand exceeds one of those budgets?… more

content: People are giving each other advice today that sounds like this:Don't get married. Don't have kids. Don't take a loan. Don't buy anything. Save every rupee. Just survive.I understand where that fear comes from.When layoffs, PIPs and restructures keep showing up on your feed, your brain naturally starts preparing for the worst.But if you have a job today, you do not need to start eating one meal less.You need to build enough financial breathing room that one bad news does not turn into a family crisis.A few simple rules will definetly help:→ Keep total EMIs around 30 to 40% of take-home pay if your situation allows it. A high salary can disappear faster than a high EMI.→ Build at least 6 months of essential expenses in cash or something easily accessible. If you have dependents, a single income, or large loans, aim higher for 12+ months. → Have health insurance beyond whatever your employer provides, and term insurance if people financially depend on you. Jobs change. Your family's protection should not change with them.→ Know your "survival budget." If income stops tomorrow, which expenses stay, which can be reduced, and how long can you run the house without liquidating long-term investments?And please be careful with lifestyle inflation.The high paying job arrives, then comes the bigger flat, car EMI, subscriptions, expensive holidays, and suddenly a person earning very well still cannot survive three months without salary.Everyone's responsibilities are different. There is no perfect number that works for every family.The goal is just to create enough space that if life goes wrong for a few months, you have time to think instead of panic.Also, focus on the other side too.Keep learning. Keep your network alive. content: Most engineers think you become a leader by getting promoted. You become a leader the day people start bringing you problems before their manager. Title comes later. They earn it in ways that do not get logged in performance reviews.Following up on a decision without being asked. Giving credit when nobody is watching. Doing the small unglamorous thing that keeps the team from breaking on a Friday afternoon.The industry loves to talk about leadership as a career milestone. RAG is not a feature.It is a series of engineering decisions that compound across 5 layers.Get one layer wrong and the whole system degrades silently.𝟏. 𝐒𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐜𝐞 𝐒𝐞𝐥𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧: Index the wrong sources and no retrieval strategy saves you.𝟐. 𝐂𝐡𝐮𝐧𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐌𝐞𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐝: Fixed, semantic, or hierarchical. Each has a different failure mode.𝟑. 𝐄𝐦𝐛𝐞𝐝𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐌𝐨𝐝𝐞𝐥: General-purpose encoders underperform on specialized domain queries.𝟒. 𝐈𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐱 𝐓𝐲𝐩𝐞: HNSW for speed. IVF for memory efficiency. Flat for maximum precision.𝟓. 𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐁𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐞𝐧𝐝: Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate, or pgvector. Scale determines the answer.𝟔. 𝐌𝐞𝐭𝐚𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐚 𝐒𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐠𝐲: Define filter fields before ingestion. Retrofitting metadata is painful.𝟕. 𝐑𝐞𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐯𝐚𝐥 𝐌𝐨𝐝𝐞: Dense alone misses keyword matches. Hybrid covers both signal types.𝟖. 𝐃𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐌𝐞𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐜: Cosine for normalized embeddings. Dot product for raw similarity scores.𝟗. 𝐅𝐢𝐥𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐒𝐜𝐨𝐩𝐞: Pre-filter improves speed. Post-filter improves recall. Know the trade-off.𝟏𝟎. 𝐓𝐨𝐩-𝐊 𝐕𝐚𝐥𝐮𝐞: Too low and you miss valid answers. Too high and you flood the context window.𝟏𝟏. 𝐑𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐤𝐞𝐫 𝐒𝐞𝐥𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧: Cross-encoders improve accuracy but add latency. Choose deliberately.𝟏𝟐. 𝐒𝐜𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐓𝐡𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐡𝐨𝐥𝐝: No minimum bar means low-confidence results reach the LLM every time.𝟏𝟑. 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐱𝐭 𝐁𝐮𝐝𝐠𝐞𝐭: Retrieved content must fit the token window without truncating key chunks.𝟏𝟒. 𝐅𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤 𝐒𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐠𝐲: Define what happens at zero results before it happens in production.𝟏𝟓. 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐬: Force the LLM to answer from retrieved context only, not from weights.𝟏𝟔. 𝐎𝐛𝐬𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐜𝐤: Trace every retrieval decision or you cannot debug what went wrong.RAG is not plug and play. It is an engineering discipline with 16 decisions that compound.P.S. Which of these decisions is your team making without a clear strategy?Credit:- Manas DasguptaFollow Your Growth Buddies for more insights… moreThe most interesting part is how many moving pieces sit between raw information and a useful answer. Reliability is rarely decided by one component alone.

content: OpenAI and Anthropic are probably two of the hardest software companies to get into right now, even beyond the usual FAANG grind.I found one Anthropic interview experience that makes the bar very clear. The engineer had 10+ years of experience across backend, AI, and distributed systems.He got rejected before the first interview.If you're curious about what Anthropic is testing, check this out: 1/ This wasn't the usual LeetCode grindThe OA was 90 minutes.You start with one small in-memory system and keep extending it through 4 levels.Think:Level 1: basic banking operationsLevel 2: add more rulesLevel 3: introduce more stateLevel 4: now entities can merge, but their old history still needs to remain correctSo every decision you make early comes back later.Write messy code in Level 1 and Level 4 becomes hell.That's very different from solving two unrelated DSA questions and moving on. 2/ No AI. No searching. Not even another browser tab.This part surprised me. He said AI was completely banned and you weren't even allowed to switch tabs.Which means Claude can’t do this for you in here. 3/ The hardest part wasn't algorithmsIt was changing an existing system without breaking what already worked.That's much closer to actual engineering.You need to keep track of state, history, edge cases, data models and old behaviour while requirements keep changing underneath you.The candidate said historical state after merging entities was where most of the difficulty came from. 4/ His preparation was much smarter than "do more LeetCode"He practised three systems before the OA:→ Wallet / banking system→ In-memory filesystem→ In-memory databaseHe asked ChatGPT to create progressive requirements, wrote the implementations himself, then used AI to generate tests against his code.That's a really good prep loop.Build → test → find what breaks → extend the requirements → repeat. 5/ And yes, 580/600 still wasn't enoughAnother person in the same thread even said they got 600/600 and were rejected without an interview.So clearly the OA score is only one signal. Sleep gets worse. Stamina drops. Your back starts hurting. Stairs feel harder. You tell yourself you can fix it in six months whenever you finally "have time."Then six months pass. The problem is that life rarely clears the calendar for you.Work will still be there.Family responsibilities will still be there.There will always be another deadline, stressful month, or reason to postpone yourself.At some point, you have to carry your health alongside everything else.And once you do you will realize that taking care of your body is often what gives you the capacity to carry everything else better.You think you are too tired to exercise, but regular movement can improve the very energy you feel you are missing.You think one hour away from work is expensive, until poor health starts taking entire days away from you.This post is not about body shaming anyone.A belly, a number on a weighing scale, or how somebody looks tells you very little about the full picture.This is simply about paying attention before your body forces you to.Because when life is going well, you have a hundred problems. content: TypeSafe gives you $5 of API credit when you sign upAt Jev's pricing, that is basically never ending…Why? Because Jev is priced at $0.042 per million input tokensAnd output is freeSo that $5 credit gives you roughly 119 million input tokens. That is why people are joking that they will pass their Jev credits down to their children, haha. What makes it interesting is that Jev just makes decisions. You give it context, plus a fixed set of options, and it tells you what to do nextThat is exactly why it is so useful. Instead of paying a big model to generate a wall of text you will barely use, Jev can do the small, high-volume decisions inside the workflow, for example: → which support team gets this ticket→ which model should handle this prompt→ is this output safe or risky→ should the agent call this tool or not→ which ad fits this category→ which alert is real and which one is noise→ which rows should I keep, rank, or dropPeople are already using it for browser agents, model routing, Postgres filtering, security workflows, and 10s of other use cases. And the economics are what driving all the hype behind Jev. content: AI is making software engineers more productive and more exhausted at the same time.And I think the reason is pretty obvious to everyone. We are stuck in this weird middle ground where AI is good enough to delegate real work to, but not reliable enough to completely forget about once we delegate it.If my manager gives me something and I say, "I'll take care of it," they can mentally remove it from their plate.They trust that I will either finish it or come back if something goes wrong.AI does not give you that feeling yet. You can tell an agent, "Fix this bug, update the tests, and open the PR."It says, "Sure." But somewhere in your head, the task is still running.You're thinking: Did it misunderstand the requirement?Did it break something unrelated?Did it actually run the tests?So you keep checking. Now repeat that across an entire workday.This is why people say working with agents for eight hours leaves their brain fried.And the expectation has gone up at the same time because now everyone assumes AI should make you faster.The worst version of this is running 15 or 20 agents simultaneously.Having 20 agents making you 20x productive sounds awesome until you realize you have basically, become the manager of 20 very fast junior employees who constantly need permissions, context, reviews and corrections.Of course your brain is exhausted.I think the better way work is this: Have one coordinating agent manage the work, let it finish meaningful chunks, and review those chunks in batches.Reduce the number of conversations your brain has to keep alive.Remove the cognitive load as much as you can, we're not built for context switching. If your setup requires you to watch 20 terminals all day, you have probably just automated the work and kept all the stress.… moreThere is also a trust calibration problem. If an agent is right 95% of the time, that sounds amazing. But if you do not know which 5% is wrong, you still have to inspect almost everything. Reliability is not just accuracy. content: Your pipeline can process every event and still produce the wrong table.Maybe a retry creates a duplicate.Maybe a bad record blocks a batch.Or a crash happens after the write but before the offset is saved.Here are 8 patterns that make the result recoverable:Transactional outbox→ Save the business change and an outbox event in one database transaction. Avoid the "DB succeeded, publish failed" gap.Change data capture→ Read committed changes from the source log instead of scanning entire tables repeatedly. Plan for bootstrap and schema changes.Idempotent sink→ Writing event 42 twice produces the same final state as writing it once. Use a stable key or transaction boundary.Checkpointing→ Persist progress so a failed job resumes from a known point. Coordinate the checkpoint with the output write.Dedup window→ Remember recent event IDs and drop repeats. Define how long an ID must stay in state.Watermarks→ Hold event-time windows open long enough for expected late arrivals. The allowed lateness is a product decision.Dead-letter queue→ Move a permanently bad record aside so healthy data keeps flowing. Alert on the queue or it becomes a hiding place.Replay and backfill→ Keep enough source history to rebuild a wrong output after code or schema changes. Know which table version readers should see.… more

content: This video would not exist if there wasn't a huge audience for it.You can criticise the creator for making Class 8th to IIT content, but the bigger question is why a 13 or 14-year-old feels they need a four-year battle plan for one entrance exam in the first place.That demand comes from us.Parents, schools, coaching culture, relatives, social media, success stories. Somewhere along the way, JEE stopped being an exam and became a symbol of intelligence, security, status, and even your worth.And I want to be fair here.Preparing seriously for JEE can teach you a lot. Discipline, focus, consistency, problem solving, and a lot more. Those are valuable skills even if you never enter an IIT.But there is a very important difference between:"I am preparing hard for JEE."and"My entire future depends on cracking JEE."The second one is where things become unhealthy.A 15-year-old should be allowed to fail a mock test without feeling like life is slipping away. They should be allowed to discover that maybe they love physics, maybe they hate engineering, maybe their path changes completely at 19.One exam should not carry the emotional weight of an entire life.Creators are often responding to what society already rewards. If parents are searching for "JEE preparation from Class 8," somebody will make that video.So maybe the conversation should be bigger than blaming one YouTuber. We need to stop teaching children that success has one entrance gate.Aim for IIT if you genuinely want it. Work hard. Give it everything.But let JEE remain a part of your life. Do not make it your whole life before life has even properly started.

content: It’s a different kind of satisfaction when you understand why something works instead of just getting it to work.I think this is one of the best ways you can use AI while learning software engineering.When I was learning to code, I would have loved a tool that could look at a compiler error, explain what it meant, and then let me fix it myself.Quite different from saying, "Claude, fix this."Because when you write the code yourself, struggle with it, and finally understand why it works, you build instincts that stay with you much longer.And those instincts help you during you career. They show up when production breaks, when AI gives you code that looks correct but is subtly wrong.They also show up when two solutions both work, but one of them is going to create a nightmare six months later.This is where I think a lot of young developers are getting stuck now.AI has become so deeply embedded in the workflow that some people have not written good code by hand in months. The moment they try to go back, there is anxiety."What if I am slower now?""What if I forgot the syntax?""What if I cannot solve this without help?"That is a genuine feeling.And I do not think the answer is to stop using AI.The better balance is:→ Use AI to explain the error→ Ask it why the bug happened→ Ask for hints before solutions→ Compare your approach with its approach→ Make it challenge your assumptions→ Let it review what you wrote after you finishFor learning, this is incredibly powerful.You still get the speed and access of AI, but the actual thinking stays with you.And later, when you are working professionally with agents all day, that foundation becomes the thing that lets you judge their output instead of blindly trusting it.AI can help you get unstuck. Don’t let it skip the part where your brain actually learns why the system works, especially when you’re learning. I’m not writing code by hand now, but I’ve written enough to understand, and at times I’ll just fix the errors myself instead of spinning up an agent. That feeling still hits different, haha.
